_purpose: MODELED city service unit costs. Manual, reviewed input (mill-rates pattern) — NOT auto-fetched, NOT part of the weekly refresh. Never label any result here 'total city cost' (police/parks/drainage unmeasured). Sourced on Peter's laptop 2026-07-15 (edmonton.ca unreachable from the Oracle box); the transportation-ops block added 2026-08-03.
_two_bases: ⚠️ THIS FILE CARRIES TWO INCOMPATIBLE COST BASES AND THEY MUST NEVER BE SUMMED OR COMPARED. (1) LIFECYCLE — roadway_om_renewal, $50/road-m/yr, O&M + capital renewal annualized over a 50-year life; feeds cost_roads_life_per_acre. (2) OPERATING — the three *_ops blocks below, annual maintenance + snow clearing with NO capital replacement; feeds transport_cost_ops_per_acre. The SAME road metres cost $50/m/yr on basis (1) and $9.32/m/yr on basis (2) — a 5.4x gap (it was 10.8x until the 2026-09-06 operating re-scope; roadway_ops.rescoped_2026_09_06), both shipping in the same served GeoJSON. That is why every operating column carries the _ops suffix. A bikeway LIFECYCLE figure analogous to roadway_om_renewal STILL DOES NOT EXIST and is a separate open item — as of 2026-08-04 its CAPITAL half is sourced and verified (see bikeway_capital, $452,065/km) but no SERVICE LIFE is published, so there is nothing to annualize over and no third basis has been introduced here. ⚠️ NOTE roadway_renewal ($38/m/yr, added 2026-08-07) IS NOT A THIRD BASIS EITHER — it is basis (1) decomposed into its published O&M ($12) and renewal ($38) halves, which sum back to the $50. The rule it needs is different from the two-bases rule: never sum roadway_renewal WITH roadway_om_renewal, because that double-counts renewal rather than mixing bases. Meanwhile $178/km/yr is an operating-maintenance line, NOT an all-in rate (at 50 years it totals $8,900/km for build + all replacement, and the same source puts snow clearing on that network at 113x the rate — see bikeway_ops.rejected_lifecycle_reading).

roadway_om_renewal.applies_to: the collector+local centreline metres in road_m_per_acre (arterials excluded from the metric)

source.page: City of Edmonton — Development Impact on Infrastructure

published_figures_per_km_neighbourhood_r.life_years: usually 25, extended to 50 with proper maintenance
published_figures_per_km_neighbourhood_r.set_aside_rule: ≈3% of infrastructure value per year to operate/maintain/renew/replace

roadway_om_renewal.derivation: lifecycle O&M ($600k) + renewal ($1.9M) = $2.5M per km, annualized over the 50-year (well-maintained) life -> $50,000/km/yr = $50/m/yr. Peter's call 2026-07-15 (50-yr, not 25-yr).
roadway_om_renewal.cross_check: ⚠️ NOT AN INDEPENDENT CHECK — demoted 2026-09-03, do not cite it as corroboration. 3% of the $1.5M capital value ≈ $45,000/km/yr ≈ $45/m/yr, which LOOKS like a second opinion agreeing with $50. It is not. The City defines its 3% ON THE SAME PAGE as covering 'operate, maintain, renew and replace' — i.e. exactly the $600k + $1.9M bundle over exactly this life, so it is the same arithmetic restated. This file already computes the bundle's own implied rate as 3.33%/yr (see bikeway_capital.three_percent_rule_does_not_transfer); $45,000 vs $50,000 is the gap between a rounded 3% and the actual 3.33%, not an agreement between two measurements. The rule is asset-specific in the source anyway — the same page assigns fire stations 'at least 6%' — so the road 3% is a property of this worked example, not a general law that could confirm it. ⚠️ WHAT SURVIVES: it still DISCRIMINATES the 50-year reading from the 25-year one directionally (3.33%/yr vs 6.67%/yr), because the life is the only free variable. That much is usable and is the honest version of the claim. What is NOT usable is calling it independent. The $50 value does not change and nothing served moves; this key has no code consumers.
roadway_om_renewal.sensitivity: 25-year (unmanaged) life would double this to ~$100/m/yr. Calibrated to NEIGHBOURHOOD (local) roads; collectors cost somewhat more per metre, so this is a mild lower bound for the collector share.
roadway_om_renewal.caveat: MODELED, roads-only. A published per-km lifecycle unit cost applied uniformly — not Edmonton's actual per-segment spend.

roadway_renewal._status: ⚠️ NOT A THIRD BASIS — this is the CAPITAL-RENEWAL HALF of roadway_om_renewal, the same basis (1) split into its two published components. $12 O&M + $38 renewal = the $50/m/yr above. ⚠️ NEVER SUM roadway_renewal WITH roadway_om_renewal: that double-counts the renewal term. Only ONE of the two may appear in any given figure. Inert by construction — load_unit_costs reads roadway_om_renewal / fire_response / roadway_ops / bikeway_ops / transit_ets and does NOT read this block, so no served column changes; it exists for ward/neighbourhood renewal reporting (tools/ward_rollup.py).
roadway_renewal.units: dollars per road-metre per year (MODELED, capital renewal only)
roadway_renewal.applies_to: the collector+local centreline metres in road_m_per_acre — arterials EXCLUDED, so any total built from this is a PARTIAL network by construction and must be labelled as such
roadway_renewal.derivation: renew_and_replace ($1,900,000/km, roadway_om_renewal.source.published_figures_per_km_neighbourhood_road) annualized over the same 50-year well-maintained life Peter chose 2026-07-15 -> $38,000/km/yr = $38/m/yr. The complementary O&M half is $600,000/km / 50 yr = $12/m/yr.
roadway_renewal.why_the_renewal_half_alone: Decided 2026-08-07 (Peter). A renewal-fund framing is about CAPITAL RENEWAL, so the renewal term is the one that answers it. Publishing the $12 O&M half instead would put a SECOND recurring road number beside roadway_ops' $4.635/m/yr — both non-capital, both annual, ~2.6x apart, different sources — which is exactly the arithmetically-true/descriptively-false collision _two_bases exists to prevent. $38 renewal does not compete with $4.635 operating because they are not the same kind of number.
roadway_renewal.citywide_scale: Against the pipeline's own collector+local metres (~3,644 km on the 406 served hoods, 2026-08-07), this is ~$138.5M/yr. ⚠️ That is an annual renewal REQUIREMENT, not a funding GAP: a gap is requirement minus what is already funded, and this project has no data on the funded side. Do NOT compare it to a published citywide infrastructure-gap figure as though the two were the same quantity.
roadway_renewal.caveat: MODELED, roads-only, collector+local only. Inherits every caveat on roadway_om_renewal: a published per-km unit cost applied uniformly, calibrated to neighbourhood roads, not Edmonton's actual per-segment renewal spend.

source.⚠️_TWO_SOURCES_TWO_VINTAGES: This rate's two halves come from DIFFERENT publications of DIFFERENT years, and that is deliberate — the maintenance half was re-scoped onto the City's own published program on 2026-09-06 (see rescoped_2026_09_06) while the snow half kept its source. Maintenance is FY2017; snow is 2025. The maintenance half is therefore stated in 2017 dollars and is NOT escalated, which is one of the two reasons this basis is a FLOOR (see floor). Do not quote the pair as one vintage.

maintenance.publication: City of Edmonton Open Budget portal, `Roadway Maintenance` operating program, FY2017 — $65,671,000. A SEPARATE program from `Snow and Ice Control` ($63,709,000), so it is maintenance-only and does not double-count the snow half below. See data/DATA.md §17 for the portal, its two rename eras and the +1.31% portal-vs-PDF gap.
maintenance.retrieved: 2026-09-05, fetched from the Oracle box with certifi (this box's CA bundle is stale). Reproduction in docs/FINDINGS_roadway_maintenance_rate.md §6.
maintenance.why_FY2017: ⚠️ 2017 is the ONLY year Edmonton published a roads-only maintenance program. It was re-cut in 2018 into `Infrastructure Maintenance` (which also covers sidewalks, pathways and bridges, so using it would double-count) and again in 2026 into `Mobility Infrastructure Services`. Clean scope was chosen over matching vintage — the same call DATA.md §16 made for the budget pod.
maintenance.not_escalated: ⚠️ DELIBERATELY UNESCALATED. Escalating by the Parks & Roads Services branch's own FY2017→FY2025 growth (1.3357x) would give ~$7,974/km, but that is BRANCH-level growth applied to a PROGRAM-level figure — a proxy, not a deflator — and FY2025 is the series MAXIMUM (FY2026 gives 1.2551x). The unescalated figure needs no assumption at all and is the safer one to publish. It also makes this half an understatement, never an overstatement.

snow_and_ice_control.publication: Taproot Edmonton, 'Why it costs so much more to clear snow from sidewalks, bike lanes than roads', by Stephanie Swensrude, quoting City of Edmonton infrastructure field operations supervisor Valerie Dacyk directly. Published 2025-08-29.
snow_and_ice_control.retrieved: 2026-08-03 (relayed, not fetched from the Oracle box). ⚠️ DATE CORRECTED 2026-09-03: this block read '2026-08-29 reporting date as supplied' and the article is in fact 2025-08-29 — the relayed date was a YEAR LATE. Verified by fetching the URL above, which also confirms the $1,285/km, $178/km and $67M figures and the Dacyk attribution. The 'as supplied' hedge is what made the error findable — keep hedging relayed dates that way.
snow_and_ice_control.snow_derivation: ~$36.85M annual road snow-clearing / ~11,000 km citywide road network = $3,350/km/yr
snow_and_ice_control.still_sourced_here: ⚠️ This article ALSO states the $1,285/km 'maintenance' figure this block shipped until 2026-09-06. That figure is gone from the rate but the article is not discredited — its TOTALS reconcile (roads snow $36.85M + path snow $30.15M = 99.2% of the portal's published `Snow and Ice Control` program), which is exactly the contrast that exposed the maintenance line. Keep the snow half.

roadway_ops.caveat: OPERATING ONLY. Both halves are annual upkeep; capital reconstruction is carried separately (40-year full-reconstruction cycle, neighbourhood lump sums) and is NOT in this number. Do NOT compare this to bikeway_ops as if either were all-in, and do NOT sum it with roadway_om_renewal — see _two_bases.
roadway_ops.rescoped_2026_09_06: ⚠️ THE MAINTENANCE HALF WAS $1,285/km UNTIL 2026-09-06, WHEN IT WAS RE-SCOPED ONTO THE CITY'S OWN PUBLISHED PROGRAM (4.65x higher). value 4.635 -> 9.32, maintenance 1285 -> 5970. Peter's call; full record in docs/FINDINGS_roadway_maintenance_rate.md, one-line index entry in docs/DECISIONS.md. WHY: (1) THE SPLIT TREATMENT — DATA.md §16 retired `$1,285/km x ~11,000 km = $14.135M` as ~5x too low on 2026-08-04 and replaced it with this same published program, so the repo was rejecting a figure in the budget pod while shipping it as half of a public map layer. data/city_budget_context.json already carried the $65,671,000 line. (2) $1,285 FAILED THE PROJECT'S OWN TEST — it carries the same 'replace, repair, and maintain' phrase, from the same sentence of the same article, as the $178/km this file rejects below, and fails the same set-aside test (0.086%/yr, 39x low against the City's 3.33%/yr rule). (3) THE 2.6x OPEN GAP DISSOLVES — against the $12/m/yr lifecycle O&M half this rate now sits at 1.29x, and the two sources do not disagree about roads. WHAT THE RE-SCOPE COST: an arterial blend in the maintenance half as well as the snow half (denominator_mismatch now covers both) and a mixed vintage (source.⚠️_TWO_SOURCES_TWO_VINTAGES). Both push the same way as the pre-existing snow caveat, and both are why this basis is still a FLOOR. ⚠️ WHAT $1,285 ACTUALLY MEASURED REMAINS UNKNOWN — the article gives it no denominator and no scope, and no clean decomposition of the published program reproduces it (materials-only $1,634/km is closest, still 1.27x off). It was not re-scoped because a better reading of it was found; it was dropped because nothing supports reading it as total road maintenance. Do not reintroduce it with an invented scope.
roadway_ops.denominator_mismatch: ⚠️ BOTH HALVES ARE CITYWIDE BLENDS OVER THE SAME ~11,000 km, AND BOTH INCLUDE ARTERIALS. Arterials are priority-cleared and more heavily maintained, and cost more per km than locals, so applying either blend to the collector+local metres in road_m_per_acre almost certainly OVERSTATES the local-road term. This applied to the snow half from the start; the maintenance half inherited it in the 2026-09-06 re-scope, which is the price that call paid and is recorded as such. ⚠️ It cuts the OPPOSITE way from the unescalated FY2017 vintage — see floor — so the two known errors in this rate have opposite signs and neither has been sized. The 11,000 km denominator itself is deliberately NOT imported anywhere in the spatial pipeline; only the per-km rates are used.
roadway_ops.floor: ⚠️ TREAT THIS BASIS AS A FLOOR, symmetric with the lifecycle basis (which the NRP reconstruction cross-check established as one — docs/FINDINGS_nrp_reconstruction_cross_check.md). The 2026-09-06 re-scope RAISED the floor 2.011x; it did not remove the framing. The maintenance half is unescalated FY2017 money against a 2025 snow half, and the City's own branch-level growth would put it 1.26-1.34x higher. ⚠️ The arterial blend in denominator_mismatch pushes the other way, so 'floor' is a judgement about which error is larger, not an arithmetic bound — do not present it as a proven lower limit.

source.publication: Taproot Edmonton, as above, quoting City of Edmonton infrastructure field operations staff
source.retrieved: 2026-08-03 (relayed, not fetched from the Oracle box)
source.snow_derivation: ~$30.15M annual active-pathway snow clearing / ~1,500 km cleared network = $20,100/km/yr

bikeway_ops.derivation: ($178 maintenance + $20,100 snow) / km / yr = $20,278/km/yr = $20.278/m/yr. Bikeway costs 4.4x roads PER METRE on this basis — cheap to maintain, expensive to clear (a 24-hour bare-pavement service standard).
bikeway_ops.rejected_lifecycle_reading: ⚠️ A relayed brief proposed reading $178/km/yr as an ALL-IN lifecycle rate (from the phrasing 'replace, repair, and maintain') and hardcoding it as the bikeway analogue of roadway_om_renewal's $50/m/yr. REJECTED 2026-08-03 on arithmetic: (a) it derives from ~$0.27M/yr spread over ~1,500 km, which cannot be replacing that network; (b) the same source puts snow clearing on the same network at $20,100/km/yr — 113x the supposed all-in build-and-replace rate; (c) at a 50-year life it totals $8,900/km for construction plus all replacement; (d) against the City's own set-aside rule of ~3%/yr of asset value (see roadway_om_renewal.source), it is 0.039%/yr, 85x low — ⚠️ CORRECTED 2026-09-05: this read '~0.09%/yr, ~33x low', computed against an implied ~$200,000/km asset value because it was written 2026-08-03, the day BEFORE bikeway_capital ($452,065/km) was sourced, and was never updated to it. The rejection is STRENGTHENED, not weakened; only the multiple was stale. ⚠️ The same test on the $1,285/km ROAD rate — same sentence, same article — gives 0.086%/yr, 39x low; see roadway_ops.published_program_contradiction. It is an operating-maintenance line. A TRUE bikeway lifecycle figure remains an OPEN item. Its capital-cost-per-km half was sourced and verified 2026-08-04 (bikeway_capital); only the SERVICE LIFE is still missing, and it is not published anywhere on edmonton.ca — see bikeway_capital.life_not_published.
bikeway_ops.denominator_mismatch: ⚠️ The $20,100/km snow rate is a BLEND over a ~1,500 km cleared network that the source defines as 'bike lanes, multi-use paths, public pedestrian squares, bus stops, LRT platforms, and staircases' — substantially NOT dedicated bikeway. Our numerator (bike_m_per_acre, ~981 km) is dedicated cycling assets only. Rate and numerator therefore do not describe the same network, and the direction of the resulting error is NOT knowable from the source. This is DATA.md §15's 'the exclusions are the metric' resurfacing on the cost side.
bikeway_ops.not_sidewalks: Sidewalks are a separate, non-overlapping category (~5,776 km, ~$5.9M/yr ops) and are NOT in this metric or in the 1,500 km snow denominator.

bikeway_capital._status: ⚠️ PARTIAL INPUT — NOT A RATE, NOT CONSUMED BY ANYTHING. This is the capital half of the still-open bikeway-lifecycle item, recorded so the sourcing is never re-hunted. It is $/km of ASSET VALUE, not $/m/yr. It CANNOT be turned into a lifecycle rate until a SERVICE LIFE exists, and no Edmonton service life for bikeways or shared pathways is published (searched 2026-08-04 — see life_not_published). load_unit_costs reads only roadway_om_renewal / fire_response / roadway_ops / bikeway_ops / transit_ets, so this block is inert by construction.
bikeway_capital.units: dollars per kilometre of bike route, CAPITAL CONSTRUCTION ONLY (blended citywide)

source.document: City of Edmonton — Edmonton Bike Plan Implementation Guide (2021–2026, February 2021), §1.2 'How much will it cost to expand the network?', TABLE 3: Bike Network Cost by Area
source.retrieved: 2026-08-04 (fetched directly on Peter's laptop; edmonton.ca is unreachable from the Oracle box — DATA.md §13)
source.table: Central 28 km / $20,000,000; Urban 126 km / $73,300,000; Suburban redeveloping 254 km / $97,500,000; Suburban developing+future growth 270 km / $115,700,000. TOTAL 678 km / $306,500,000.
source.scope_quote: 'These costs represent the capital costs to construct bike lanes and do not include maintenance costs.' Blended costs include construction materials, signalization where historically required, and transit stop; they EXCLUDE bridge upgrades and inflation.

bikeway_capital.derivation: $306,500,000 / 678 km = $452,065/km, the citywide blended capital cost.
bikeway_capital.verified: Table 3 was checked rather than relayed (2026-08-04): every row's implied $/km falls inside its own stated band (Central $714,286 in $650k–790k; Urban $581,746 in $500k–720k; Suburban redeveloping $383,858 and developing $428,519, both in $365k–495k); the suburban subtotal (524 km / $213,200,000) adds; and the prose figure for the City-borne redeveloping share ($190,800,000 = 20.0 + 73.3 + 97.5M) reconciles exactly.
bikeway_capital.life_not_published: ⚠️ NO EDMONTON SERVICE LIFE FOR A BIKEWAY OR SHARED PATHWAY IS PUBLISHED. Checked 2026-08-04: the 'Development Impact on Infrastructure' page (roads and fire stations only), the Bike Plan and its Implementation Guide, the 2025 Infrastructure Report, the Infrastructure State-and-Condition / Inventory / Management-Tools pages, and the 2023 Capital Asset Management Audit. The Bike Plan's own action 9.6.2(a) is to 'ESTABLISH a long-term asset management program ... to maintain, repair, and replace the bike route surface', i.e. the City flagged this as not yet existing. ⚠️ DO NOT substitute the sidewalk-reconstruction figure: 'amortized for 20 years' there is a LOCAL IMPROVEMENT TAX LEVY TERM, not an asset life — the same category error as reading $178/km/yr as a lifecycle rate.
bikeway_capital.three_percent_rule_does_not_transfer: ⚠️ THE CITY'S ~3%/yr SET-ASIDE RULE IS FALSIFIED FOR BIKEWAYS BY THIS PROJECT'S OWN DATA, and must not be used to shortcut the missing service life. Roads' own implied rate is ($600k O&M + $1.9M renewal) / $1.5M capital / 50 yr = 3.33%/yr. Applied to $452,065/km it allows $15,069/km/yr for ALL O&M plus renewal — but the measured bikeway_ops is $20,278/km/yr, 1.35x that ENTIRE allowance, before a dollar of capital renewal. Bikeway cost is driven by a winter SERVICE STANDARD (24-hour bare pavement), not by asset value, so a value-proportional rule cannot describe it. Note the rule is asset-specific in the source anyway: the same page assigns fire stations 'at least 6%'.
bikeway_capital.facility_mix_mismatch: ⚠️ Table 3 blends the facility mix likely to be built in FUTURE, while bike_m_per_acre measures the EXISTING dedicated stock, and the two mixes differ sharply. Our 981 km is 82.2% Shared Pathway and 89.8% off-road pathway/trail, with only 0.8% Local Street Bikeway — whereas Table 3's blend leans on the cheap on-street types (local street bikeways, painted lanes) that DATA.md §15 largely excludes. Direction is knowable here, unlike the two snow-rate mismatches above: $452,065/km most likely UNDERSTATES the replacement value of our network. This is DATA.md §15's 'the exclusions are the metric' resurfacing a third time.
bikeway_capital.cross_check_program_budget: The 2023–2026 Capital Budget's Active Transportation Network Expansion is $100,000,000 for 35 km built (2024–2025) plus 33 km planned (2026+) = 68 km, i.e. ~$1.47M/km — 3.3x this blended rate. NOT a contradiction to resolve by averaging: that is a whole-PROGRAM budget (design, engineering, contingency, land) against Table 3's construction-only unit cost, and ATNE builds exclusively inside Anthony Henday in the dearer Central/Urban contexts. Recorded as an upper bound on what a delivered km actually costs, not as a competing value.

transit_ets.chosen_numerator: GROSS bus+LRT (436,605), matching fire_response's gross choice. ⚠️ DATS ($31,966K) is DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED: it is door-to-door paratransit and generates NO scheduled stop-events, so allocating it by transit_dep_total would charge paratransit cost to hoods purely for having bus/LRT service.
transit_ets.divisor: citywide mean-weekday scheduled stop-events — compute from the pipeline's OWN transit frame total so numerator and denominator match the transit_dep_per_acre numerator (do NOT hardcode). Same rule as fire_response.divisor.
transit_ets.no_mode_split_needed: Bus and LRT are one budget line in every public Edmonton document, and this allocation does not need them separated: a combined budget over combined departures is exactly right. load_transit.py does expose transit_dep_bus / transit_dep_lrt, but the composite uses transit_dep_total only. Do NOT introduce a peer-benchmark LRT-vs-bus cost ratio to 'fix' this — there is nothing to fix.
transit_ets.caveat: MODELED demand ALLOCATION of a mostly-FIXED budget, exactly like fire_response: a hood with twice the scheduled service does not cost ETS twice — most transit cost is standing network capacity. Carry this caveat in UI copy. Scheduled supply is NOT ridership.
transit_ets.vintage_mismatch: ⚠️ This is a 2025 figure while fire_response is 2026 Approved. Accepted 2026-08-03 as documented rather than blocking. MOOT since 2026-09-05: the fire budget feeds no column at all (fire_response._status), so there is no mismatch left to carry.
transit_ets.why_this_allocation_survived_the_audit: ⚠️ READ THIS BEFORE PROPOSING A FOURTH ALLOCATION. This term has the SAME SHAPE as the fire term retired on 2026-09-05 — a citywide budget divided by a citywide count and charged to land — and it survived because of WHAT is being allocated, not how. ETS CHOOSES the schedule and its costs scale with service-hours (drivers, fuel, vehicles): a supply allocated by supply. Fire is standing capacity (halls, crews) allocated by DEMAND, so a hood with twice the dispatches does not cost the City twice. An allocation of a fixed capacity budget by a demand count is the pattern that failed. docs/FINDINGS_services_cost_lens_verdict.md section 4.
